I was interrupted in my speech by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) who pointed out to me at that time that there were only three members from the island of Montreal present in the house. Mr. Speaker, I had indeed noticed it. I am not as blind as some hon. members opposite who do not see the importance of that problem, etc.-

There is one point that I do not think should go unanswered. The hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois) said there were no members on the government side from Montreal present during the debate.
I never said such a thing.
I should like to point out that throughout the whole debate my colleague the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) was here-
I admit that I also saw him.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) was also here as well as my parliamentary secretary (Mr. Mackasey) who is from Verdun-
I referred to him during my comments and I agree that he was here.
The hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel).
He is not from the island of Montreal but from the outskirts of Montreal.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: COMMENT ON STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT DE GAULLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement commenting on one made yesterday in Paris by General tie Gaulle, a statement made as I was leaving London to return to Canada and which I did not see until I arrived back in Canada. Perhaps it is just as well that I did not have the opportunity of reading it before I spoke in London yesterday.
Before I make that statement, Mr. Speaker, perhaps you will permit me as Prime Minister to express my appreciation for the kindness I received from the British government during our visit to London last week and for the privilege, during a very difficult time for that government, of discussing with them some matters of commonwealth and international concern. We discussed in particular the situation in Cyprus, which has remained so dangerously explosive during recent days and which, if it were permitted to explode into armed conflict between two members of NATO and on the territory of a member of the commonwealth, could have an almost fatal effect on the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
I said in my statement of July 25, 1967, Mr. Speaker, commenting on some earlier remarks of the president of the French republic, that Canada has always had a special relationship with France, which is the motherland of so many of her citizens. I said we attached the greatest importance to our friendship with the French people; that it had been and remained the strong purpose of the government of Canada to foster that friendship. I should like to confirm those words today, Mr. Speaker.
I do not propose to deal in any detail with General de Gaulle's statement of yesterday, a statement very carefully prepared and made to the press. General de Gaulle's statement will obviously arouse discord in Canada. I am sure the people of this country will be


restrained in their response to it, as I am in mine today, so as not to serve the purposes of those who would disunite and divide our country.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: COMMENT ON STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT DE GAULLE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: COMMENT ON STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT DE GAULLE
speechtext:
I believe the statement distorted some Canadian history, misrepresented certain contemporary developments and wrongly predicted the future. This statement was not merely a commentary on Canadian domestic or foreign policies, which could have been ignored; it was an intervention in those policies by the head of a foreign state. As such it remains unacceptable. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, in this case it is intolerable that a head of a foreign state or government should recommend a course of political or constitutional action which would destroy Canadian confederation and the unity of the Canadian state.
The future of Canada, Mr. Speaker, will be decided in Canada, by Canadians.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: COMMENT ON STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT DE GAULLE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

I have confidence, and I know all members of this house have confidence, in the ability and good sense of all Canadians, French speaking or English speaking, to make the right decision. They will do it in their own way and through their own democratic process. I believe this decision will require further constitutional changes to bring our federalism up to date and to ensure, among other things, that French speaking Canadians who form one of our two founding cultural and linguistic groups, or societies if you like, will have their rights accepted and respected in Canada.
I agree also that the federal government, any federal government, should encourage and promote special and close cultural relations between French speaking Canadians and France and other French speaking countries. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, we are doing that. There should be no argument on this score except with those who wish to use these relations to destroy the federal government's responsibility for foreign affairs, and that we do not accept.
Canada is a free country and its people govern themselves. Canadians in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada have the right to exercise fully their political rights in federal and provincial elections. Self determination is no new discovery for us.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, September 29, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Cote (Longueuil)- Mr. Batten in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Post Office Act to increase by one cent the postage rates for letters posted in Canada for delivery in Canada: to provide an amended rate structure for newspapers and periodicals; and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act, more especially in relation to tenders and contracts.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR INCREASES IN POSTAL RATES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this will probably rate as one of the longest speeches ever made in this house. It was commenced on September 29 and if we had resumed consideration of this measure tomorrow it would have taken two full months. We are being asked to approve an increase in postal rates which will result in an increase in the cost of living for every Canadian and in the cost of doing business. The burden will fall chiefly on ordinary citizens because businesses will pass on the increase to the consumer while at the same time charging up additional expenses when computing their income taxes. Therefore in the case of business firms the increased rates will in reality only net the government a fraction of the amount they hope to raise. It follows then that the main burden of these increased rates

will fall on the ordinary citizens of the country. Further, I suggest that these increases should only be considered as a last resort after all other avenues have been explored.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
With this in view, Mr. Chairman, I have a few questions I should like to pose to the Postmaster General. The post office has 44,244 employees at the present time, or rather did have two months ago when my figures were prepared. In 1963 the total number of employees was 26,520. The question bothering Canadians is: Why was there a personnel increase of 69 per cent during this period while the volume of mail reportedly rose only 9 per cent? During this period the number of post offices has decreased from 11,336 to 11,172, a drop of 164.
If I may refer again to personnel, Mr. Chairman, in 1954-55 the post office operated quite efficiently with four or five so-called branches. Between then and 1959 the number of branches was increased to six with the appropriate number of directors. During this period the maximum growth of our cities took place. This was the period when the poor postman frequently found new subdivisions seemingly appearing overnight in what had previously been a cow pasture.
If ever a department did a job well, Mr. Chairman, it was in this period of maximum growth in our developing urban areas. All of this was accomplished with six branches. Now, in 1967, the post office has 13 or 14 directors, three assistant deputy ministers and five directors of personnel. I would suggest there are quite a few chiefs and that the increase in the number of these high priced individuals is taking place at an alarming rate.
This is just one of the mysteries of this department, Mr. Chairman. The fact that such a gigantic increase in personnel was not accompanied by a similar increase (a) in efficiency and (b) in volume of mail handled seems to indicate that the department probably needs considerable overhaul.
The committee has had the benefit of the minister's statement in regard to income and expenses, but I can find no accounting sheet or annual report that allows me to find out-indeed, I suggest it is impossible to find out-how much was spent on and how much was received from each kind of mail. Surely these figures exist somewhere.
In May, 1966 the minister said that he agreed with his predecessor that certain efforts should be made to follow up some of
November 28. 1967	COMMONS
the recommendations made by the Glassco royal commission. I have no way of knowing whether any of the recommendations in the Glassco commission report have actually been implemented, but I should like to refer to them for a moment. The commission made some specific recommendations, which are contained in the report on government organization volume 3, pages 350 to 351. Extensive changes were suggested in the operational scheme, the financial methods and in almost all aspects of the post office's work. The commission foresaw an annual saving of at least many millions of dollars if its recommendations were heeded.
The following, Mr. Chairman, is a summary of some of their money-saving recommendations: a time study approach in all offices, with a potential saving of $7J million; reduction of wicket staff, with a potential saving of $2.8 million; an analysis of sortation methods, with a possible saving of $4.8 million; and a thorough analysis of highway transportation, with a projected saving of $1.2 million. These in total would provide a saving of $16.3 million. Therefore my second question to the minister is: Have any of these recommendations been followed? What action has been taken toward the implementation of cost-saving programs? Has there been any real effort toward economy? All indications are that there has not been any real effort in this direction.
Having this in mind, Mr. Chairman, I think that we should delay implementation of this legislation until the minister can come before the house and say: We have saved X dollars by reducing inefficiency; we can save X dollars by making certain changes in operation and sortation. In other words, when the minister is able to say that he has actually tried to cut costs and to maintain service, only then should we support the government on this new bill.
W hether or not the post office has instituted these recommended changes we do not know. However, before the post office raises its rates to the Canadian public we should be assured that every opportunity has been taken to reduce costs. Not only is there a lack of information available but there is a stupendous amount of misleading information, and it is my guess that greatly increased efficiency should be possible.
I suggest, sir, that this bill be delayed for say six months so as to give the Postmaster General the opportunity to initiate some innovations and to streamline procedures, but 27053-302 *

We object to three things, Mr. Chairman. The increase in mail rates generally comes at a strange time, considering that the government itself is urging everyone not to increase costs. If the deficit which the government aims to meet by increasing mail rates is $30 million, as reported, then the increase will be to cover that amount and will be paid directly by the general public through increased postage rates; or by commercial establishments such as telephone and hydro companies whose bills make up a great deal of the first class mail. Can anyone imagine that business will absorb the extra $20 million, say, that it must lay out in meeting increased postal costs? I submit that as usual businesses will pass on their extra costs to the consumers, the ordinary letter writers of this country. We submit that the government's proposal to increase postage rates will increase living costs for many people. They in turn will seek to offset their increased expenses by trying to obtain a higher return in earnings.
We also object on this ground, Mr. Chairman. Though for many years first class mail, the mail of the ordinary citizen, has been paying its way and making a profit in some years, and though over the same period second and third class mail, that mail which is distributed to make a profit for someone, has been carried, at a deficit and to that extent has been subsidized by the ordinary consumer who uses first class mail, suddenly the government says. Let us wipe out the postal deficit on commercial mail largely by imposing increases on the consumers' first class mail. If postal rates are to be increased at all, surely they ought to be increased in those areas where over the years they have been proven to be too low to meet costs. I am preferring to second and third class mail.
It is said, Mr. Chairman, that first class mail is beginning to show a deficit and that it may lose money. I suggest that we should wait and see. Before increasing postage rates for consumers, why does the government not find out exactly where the deficits occur? It is too early to say exactly which way the trend is going with regard to deficits on first class mail. It is not too early to say what has

been happening to second or third class mail, that mail which has to do with commercial, private profit-making business.
The public accounts committee of the House of Commons this year made a report which contained this unanimous recommendation:
The committee first drew the matter to the attention of the house in its 1958 report-
That is almost ten years ago:
-and while minor changes have been made the annual loss has continued to increase and the committee is of the opinion that sufficient consideration has not been given to the solution of this problem. It considers it essential that the Post Office Department or parliament immediately find ways and means of covering the loss of the Post Office Department in handling second class mail . .. without this being done at the expense of other classes of mail, keeping in mind, however, the need of assistance to small independently owned newspapers circulated in rural areas.
Similar recommendations have been made by similar committees during the past six years. I make a similar recommendation today. The recommendations of the House of Commons committee, and I urge the government to heed them, have repeatedly been drawn to the attention of Postmasters General over many years. Possibly some post office difficulties have arisen owing to the high rate of turnover of Postmasters General. We have had no less than seven in the past six years.
Returning to my argument, I ask why should the Post Office Department face a deficit when ordinary first class mail has made a profit and mail having to do with private business has been carried at a loss which must be paid for by the taxpayer? I wish to quote from another source. The royal commission on publications in 1961 made this statement:
Periodicals do not carry the full cost because it is believed to be in the national interest that there be the widest distribution of periodicals and newspapers-
According to the commission, much of this deficit, which increased from $20 million in 1960 to $30 million in 1966, can be attributed to periodicals which are mailed abroad and delivered in Canada. The Canadian post office derives no revenue from the delivery of foreign second class mail. Under the terms of the universal postal convention, all governments are required to handle free of charge whatever is passed to them by foreign post offices. This arrangement is reciprocal and, in theory, equitable.
Between Canada and the United States that theory fails completely. Canadians

receive far more second class mail from abroad, largely from the United States, than they send abroad. We believe that the agreement which has brought about this situation should be renegotiated. It is not enough to say that boosting ordinary letter rates will take care of everything. We do not want to protect this situation any longer and we will not support any move that will add to the cost of living of the ordinary consumer of this country.
We ought to concern ourselves with other aspects of the post office. On the one hand the Post Office Department receives subsidies and benefits of approximately $25 million a year. These include provision for accommodation, buildings, and so on. On the other hand, the post office performs various services free of charge. Because of the free service it provides to members of the public and to members of parliament with respect to parliamentary correspondence, the post office is loaded with extra costs which according to the 1965 figures amount to approximately $4.5 million. It is not enough for us to tinker with post office rates at the retail level. In fairness we cannot increase or decrease those rates until we have a clear picture of the factors which interfere with the ability of the service to break even.
We regard the post office service as a basic service which the Canadian public has organized and which it uses and pays for. The service is a natural, public monopoly and we want it to pay its way, but that is all. We want no one class of the community to pay more or to pay less than in equity it ought to pay.
I should like the government to answer some questions so as to provide us with a clearer picture and better perspective of the dimensions of the post office service and what it costs to maintain that service.

For instance, what was the approximate value of subsidies to the post office, including accommodation, for the year 1966? What was the approximate value of the franking service and other services that were performed free of charge by the post office in 1966? What was the loss in 1966 incurred by the post office in the carrying of newspapers and magazines? What was the loss to the post office in 1966 in connection with second class mail posted in the United States for delivery in Canada? What has been the loss to the post office in the last ten years as a result of carrying Time and Reader's Digest? What
Post Office Act
was the value of printed matter imported into Canada in the last ten years and carried by our post office without remuneration under the terms of the universal post office convention?
In conclusion I summarize the position of my party with regard to the proposals to increase postal rates. We propose to let the first class mail rate alone. It is said that the rate may be resulting in a deficit. Let us study this for at least a year so as to be sure of what is happening, just as we are sure that the second class rate is incurring a loss.
In the second place we propose that the deficit which has all along been caused by subsidizing private business mailings be eliminated by increasing the rate in the area where it is low enough to cause a deficit, that is, in the second and third class rates.
Third, we ask that the government renegotiate the international treaty which has involved us in losses and bring about parity with the United States postal service in order that our consumers and publishers may not be subsidizing non-Canadian competitors.
Fourth, we want an examination-it might be through a committee or a commission or a special inquiry within the post office itself -of the various subsidies and charges borne by the postal service in order to bring out the facts and provide a clear picture showing who pays for what.
Fifth, we would like a study to be made in depth of the reported advantages of turning the post office into a public corporation, that is, a crown company operated quite separately from itinerant postmasters general.
Finally, what we in this party would like to see is a further advance in the modernization which has already taken place within the postal service. We should like its procedures and techniques brought increasingly in line with the era of technological production and distribution in which we are living. Today the post office faces a situation similar to that which the telephone companies faced a few years ago before they made their operations as automatic as possible.
We in this party aim to do what we can to bring about the most efficient service possible, the best service to the most people in the shortest time, and it is not in line with that philosophy for us to support the proposed increase in the first class mail rate.

I remember that 21 months ago, the minister had accepted his appointment with the best intentions in the world and at the time, he had made his plans known to the whole country at a press conference. It is realized today that the minister is faced with the increased cost of living.
He has to administer a department which employs a great number of workers scattered throughout the country. Those workers must pay taxes like any other, in order to meet the requirements of financiers who are asking for a larger share year after year. Taxes and charges must be raised. Our businessmen, our industrialists, through force of circumstances, have become tax collectors have to hire additional personnel and this increases costs and requires an increase in the price of their products. The present minister faces all these increases: Increases in the cost of services, rents, wages, and so on.
In view of the problems brought about by the increase in the cost of living, the Minister of Finance last spring brought down a deficit budget. Nevertheless, the Postmaster General being an intelligent man, wants to run his department on a business basis. To meet the increases in rentals of departmental premises throughout the country, to meet the demands of contractors who supply the trucks, to meet the costs of transportation either by railroad or by air, it is obviously necessary to resort to a new increase in rates. I am not opposed to this plan, because I think that it is the department where the employees work the hardest. It is also a department which generally gives excellent service.
Personally, I had the opportunity to go to Vancouver last winter and I noted that a letter mailed on Monday afternoon had been delivered in Quebec Tuesday afternoon, 24 hours later. It is also known that from Ottawa to Quebec is a twelve-hour service.
I take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. minister who uses modern means in modern times. We know that trains or trucks are still more advantageous for short distances, and that planes are better for long distances.

There still are some rural areas which are served according to old methods because certain rules apply which date back to the days of wax candles when much of the transport was handled by ox-carts. Unfortunately, a few parishes in the riding of Portneuf, which I have the honour of representing, were served that way. Their service must be improved. Some time ago, I pointed out the situation to the hon. minister and I know he will do everything in his power to give satisfaction to the people concerned.
I take this opportunity to thank him for his co-operation. I wish also to tell the minister that the part of the resolution in which I am most interested is the last paragraph, and I quote:
-to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the Act, more especially in relation to tenders and contracts.
It is interesting to note that the minister is looking for reform because the old system was really obsolete, and I could quote many examples to this effect. I have here the list of all the contractors of my region, and it is deceiving to note the numerous price differences between the various parishes for contracts providing for the same mileage and about the same number of subscribers.
This situation is caused by civil servants who work for the party. When citizens who do not belong to a specific political party are involved, however, tenders are called. That is when people try to cut each other's throat, when unemployed persons, faced with the problems of survival and an insecure future, make unreasonably low bids and are unable to discharge adequately the responsibilities involved in the circumstances, I cannot but welcome the projects of the minister for improving those methods.

To refer again to the hon. member for New Westminster, I may say that if mail is placed in a mail box in Chicago, Illinois and addressed to Vancouver or New Westminster, British Columbia, or St. John's, Newfoundland, the mail going east may come into Canada at Windsor, Ontario, and the mail going west may cross into Canada at Emerson, Manitoba. On two days in the year all the parcels are hauled to the border and the post office departments of Canada and the United States very quickly analyse and calculate the weight moving on these two days, check how far the parcels are going in either country and, using these two days as the best example, they multiply by the number of days in the year and come up with the weight of the parcel post movement from Canada to the United States and from the United States to Canada, and the distances travelled in both countries. I thought it was an insult to our graphic arts industry, which is so dependent on business from Canadian corporations, to openly approach me for business by mail which originated in the United States.
If you go into a supermarket today, Mr. Chairman, you will find that many of the labels on cans of food originate in the United States of America. The country of origin must be indicated by law. It gripes me, realizing the contribution the graphic arts industry makes to every little community, that when I buy a can of pears or peaches the label on the can bears the rather unobstru-sively printed words, "Printed in the United States of America".
A question of cold economics, of course, is involved here. In the United States there is the advantage of the over-run. More and more Canadian firms have been trying to offset the competitive advantage of the United States which merely has to run its presses a few hours longer to print labels for Canada. Canadian firms have met this competition not only by being efficient but by being on the Canadian scene. However, I am a little apprehensive, as I mentioned to the Postmaster General if the mailing rates in Canada are increased in respect of third class mail. This class of mail includes the bulk of direct mail, and any increase in rates will mean increasing the competitive advantage of direct mail originating from the United States. Many subsidiaries of international firms will once again find it expedient to send direct mail from the United States, taking advantage of United States postal rates to solicit business across Canada in competition with local representatives of the graphic arts industry.
People ask me why the government should subsidize the graphic arts industry. Why should the government subsidize small printing firms in communities across the country by carrying their mail at a low rate? It would be equally logical for the representatives of the graphic arts industry to ask why the government should subsidize those who advertise not by direct mail but on the C.B.C. This form of advertising is subsidized through the amount of money the Canadian taxpayer puts at the disposal of the C.B.C. When a program on the C.B.C. is sponsored jointly by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the Ford Motor Company, or whoever it is, we all know this is a form of

November 28, 1967
Post Office Act
subsidy to a specific type of advertising. If it is not correct to do it in one case then it is not correct to do it in another.
I therefore would not view with any tremendous degree of alarm the fact that the post office may subsidize directly or indirectly, certain segments of the graphic arts industry. Sponsors who advertise on television and on the radio are equally subsidized. In fact, the story of Canada is one of subsidy, whether it relates to farming areas, the cities, the advertising industry, the graphic arts industry, radio or television. I am sure hon. members are all familiar with the amount of subsidization that exists in this country.
I am very resentful when speakers refer, as sometimes happens, to all direct mail as being junk mail. I think this is unfair. Whether we like it or not, the amount of direct mail is increasing. Whether we like it or not, at the present moment the pulp and paper industry is badly depressed in Canada. Because of overproduction and increased competition in foreign markets, one of the godsends to firms like the E. B. Eddy Company, Abitibi and others in Canada is the amount of fine paper that is used by the graphic arts industry in the production of direct mail. We may find ourselves in the ridiculous position of trying to increase the income of the Post Office Department by increasing rates on third class mail which could result in a decrease in revenue from the 12 per cent tax that is applied to all pieces of direct mail produced in this country.
I do not pretend that every piece of direct mail produced in Canada is tasteful any more than every advertisement seen on television is tasteful. In this regard I think particularly of advertisements for the drug or pharmaceutical industry depicting men with hammers banging on their heads or their stomachs, and other similar exaggerated advertisements. They are no more tasteful than some of the direct mail which is sent out every day of the week in Canada. However, by and large the direct mail distributed in Canada is tasteful and attractive. If it is not it does not capture the imagination of the people, and if it does not do that people stop using direct mail and turn to other media of communication such as television, radio and the daily newspapers. Before hon. members condemn direct mail per se I would ask them to reflect a little and to realize the good effect that direct mail does have on the graphic arts
[Mr. Mackasey.l
industry, with the resultant good effect upon their communities as well as mine.
It is for this reason that I am not concerned about the fact that direct mail may or may not be handled at a loss to the Canadian taxpayer, any more than I am concerned about the fact that advertising on radio and television is subsidized from the huge grants we give the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. But I am concerned about any increased charge to the graphic arts industry in the form of a further increase in third class mailing rates. I say further increase because there was a substantial increase on October 1, 1967 which had to be absorbed by the graphic arts industry. This added burden, which may or may not be imposed by the Postmaster General-the resolution is not too clear about this-could very well mean the difference between further expansion in Canada of the graphic arts industry or a return to the old practice of mailing direct from the United States. This practice is to the complete and total disadvantage of the 78,000 people employed in the printing industry in Canada, as well as the fine paper merchants and others who benefit from direct mail.
I could go on, Mr. Chairman, during the short time at my disposal to point out that there is more to printing than somebody merely running a printing press. The graphic arts industry of Canada gives work to artists, to creative people, printers, translators, copywriters, proof readers, and all those other trades so familiar to the hon. member for York-Humber and other members who have been more directly associated with newspaper work.

As I mentioned, the resolution lacks information. As found at the bottom of page 2685 and the top of page 2686 of Hansard the minister said that he intends to define clearly those publications that will be carried as second class mail and those publications, weekly or otherwise, which will be relegated to third class status.
I am concerned about the following remark to be found on page 2686 of Hansard where the minister is reported to have said:
Publications which do not qualify as Canadian will come out of the second class statutory rates category.
I hold no brief for magazines which do not qualify as Canadian magazines. Hon. members who were here in 1963 may recall that
November 28, 1967

as the member for Verdun I rose in the house and suggested that Reader's Digest and Time Magazine ought to be run out of the country. I spoke for half an hour and gave my reasons. I said that since many employees of the firms that publish these magazines reside in my riding it was high time to stop procrastinating with respect to the O'Leary report, as it was known, and that we ought to decide whether these magazines were Canadian. A long debate followed and from it emerged comprehensive legislation which, among other things, prevented a further decline of Canadian magazines, reduced the possibility of United States publications competing unfairly with domestic publications and prevented Canadian newspapers from ever becoming foreign owned or dominated.
From my understanding of the law, and I expect that the minister will make a statement on second reading, first class mail rates are statutory and third and fourth class mail rates are non-statutory. I believe that everybody understands what that means. For instance, on October 1 the minister in his wisdom-and I say this objectively-decreed that matter which is classified to be carried as third and fourth class matter would be subject to an increase in postal rates from that date. It was not necessary for the minister to come before the house because any action he took was authorized under existing legislation. I expect the minister's reasons for his action were that he felt that the burden of cost of third class mail was such that these categories should pay higher postal rates. I do not object to that.
Nevertheless, I am concerned about magazines and newspapers being placed in the non-statutory category, and for this reason. They will find themselves in the onerous position of being subject to increased rates by regulations which may be applied, and these new rates imposed by regulation need not be scrutinized by the House of Commons. To make my point clear, let me say this. The minister did not say whether such publications are to be included in the third or fourth class categories. Conceivably, a new category could

The post office also attracts customers to the store who buy goods. By closing post offices the department will inevitably put many hundreds of small businessmen out of business, and these businessmen are all taxpayers. The country as a whole will not benefit from these economies and the department ought to strike a balance between the benefits that may accrue to the country from the economies of closing small post offices and the benefits that will accrue to the country from allowing taxpayers such as small businessmen to continue paying taxes. Mr. Chairman, may I say a brief word on this resolution. I agree with what has been said by my hon. friend and others in connection with the closing of many small post offices. I learned from the minister himself that it was the intention of the department to close some 700 or them across Canada. Would the hon. gentleman not give some consideration to factors other than revenue which are involved when some of these small post offices are closed? Would he not consider the services rendered and what a post office means to our small communities? Closing the post office is equivalent to destroying the identity of some of these small communities.
As hon. members can appreciate, there are common bonds which unite these communities-the church, the school, the local store and the post office. Often the local store includes the post office, and the post office has a value which cannot be measured in dollars and cents alone.
I know that several of these small post offices in my own county are to be closed. The people who use them are unhappy about the way in which the department has gone about this. There has been no opportunity for protest, just an announcement that the office will be closed. I hope the minister will not be too hasty about proceeding in this direction and that he will consider the feelings of the people who use these services. I agree we are facing economic problems but the social benefit which arises from the presence of these post offices is surely something which must be balanced against purely economic
November 28, 1987

Post Office Act
considerations. It should be remembered also that it will be necessary to pay someone to deliver the mail. In any case, the loss of post offices will affect our communities adversely to a large extent.
Turning now to another matter, when I first came to this house complaints arising from post office service could be directed to a district supervisor who lived somewhere in the area concerned. This officer would investigate individual cases and if he found evidence of fault on the part of the post office the situation would be corrected. This system worked very satisfactorily.
I do not know when the change occurred, and I am not blaming the minister for it, but I now find that the administration has been centralized and that complaints must be made to Ottawa. The service of investigation is slower, and it seems to me that the extra mileage cost must be considerable. As to the over-all service, I have received more complaints in the last 12 months than I ever received previously. Various factors may have contributed to this situation. Whether it is the attitude of the postal workers or not, I am not prepared to say. But I do believe that the removal of the district supervisors, as we knew them, has been detrimental to the service as a whole.
I hope the minister will give careful consideration to the points I have raised, particularly with respect to my plea concerning the small post offices. Some of them, I know, could be closed without any complaints arising; the people would accept the decision. But in other cases they will accept it only with the greatest unwillingness after closure has been forced upon them.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I intend to support this resolution. Indeed, I would have been pleased had the minister gone further than his proposal to raise postage rates by one cent and give effect to some amendments to the rate structure in connection with newspapers and periodicals.
From time to time I have heard the minister make remarks to the effect that it is about time we put the post office on a businesslike basis. This prospect, of course, shocks the daylight out of a great number of people who regard the post office as an institution which is independent of normal accounting. Any change intended to make it a businesslike organization fills them with consternation.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
When we are talking about the post office organization as part of a government department we must remember there was a time when the delivery of mail was very difficult and costly. That was during the days of the steamships, the pony express, and so on. Today we have so many other methods of communication that I am sure all of us must wonder whether the business of carrying messages and information is so essential that it cannot be self-sustaining like any other business, and whether it must continue to receive a government subsidy.
Let us get down to basics. In part we are talking about pesonal letters, and objection has been raised to a one cent increase in the postage rate on them. Today, with Canadians being the greatest users of telephones in the world, I doubt that any citizen sends more than one personal letter a week. In that case the increase in the rate would mean approximately 50 cents a year. If a person sends two personal letters a week the increase would be approximately $1 per year. Of course there is the Christmas card business, and I am at a loss to know whether the great increase in mail around Christmas time is so essential to our way of fife. I am sure that individuals would have no objection to paying a proper proportionate increase on their personal correspondence if the Post Office Department were organized as a crown corporation and were self-sustaining. But then we must consider business firms which might say: Well, this would be very costly to us.
Some time ago I calculated the cost of sending a letter in an ordinary law office, and I am sure the same cost would apply in most other business offices. The total cost was $2.22 taking into account the typewriter, dictating time and staff wages. That cost has now risen to $2.76 per letter. I am of the opinion that business would be much improved if it cut out about 75 per cent of its correspondence by mail and conducted its business in a more efficient manner. American corporations have gained a lot of ground in office management, and in most offices in the United States letter writing and memo writing are frowned upon. There are other methods of conducting business apart from the sending of letters.
Turning now to the question of direct mailing I point out that when it was introduced it was a good system of promotional selling, but that was 30 years ago. It was cheap and one did not expect more than a 2 per cent or 3 per cent return. In effect the

November 28, 1967
Post Office Act
government subsidizes such advertising through its postal rates. But if we are concerned about production, as I am sure the Minister of Finance will remind us on Thursday night that we should be, then business should adopt the most efficient and forwardlooking methods of selling.
I am not too concerned about direct mail advertising. Some of the people engaged in that industry will be concerned, but their talents can be used in other directions. Time and time again it has been proven that direct mail is not the best way to sell, but as long as it continues to be the cheapest way it will be used.
I would disagree with the minister a little on the question of periodicals and newspapers. If we are to sustain and promote Canadian magazines and periodicals it will be a difficult task considering the large area of Canada which our magazines have to cover and our relatively small population compared with that of the United States. I think the low postal rates for newspapers and magazines should be considered as a worth-while contribution to the promotion of Canadian magazines, but I would stress not of all magazines. We must have competition. Magazines are not good merely because they are Canadian. They must be good magazines in themselves, competitive with American magazines. When they are, then they should be supported. A magazine published in the city of New York can have a very profitable circulation in the state of New York, even in the city of New York alone. By contrast Canadian magazines have to be sent all across Canada, and therefore I favour consideration being given to our magazines and periodicals.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I seriously think it is about time we got down to putting the post office on a business basis, and not necessarily by arbitrarily setting postage rates. I support the minister in his thinking that it should be a crown corporation properly run in a businesslike way. There is a relative, comparative cost for all articles which are mailed, whether they be magazines, newspapers, personal letters or business letters. This cost can be measured accurately. One can calculate the weight of magazines, how many of them can be delivered compared with letters, and having arrived at the total I believe these articles should be charged accordingly. The same applies to direct mail and to business correspondence. If businessmen want mail delivered six times

a day, six days of the week, there is no reason why they should not pay for that privilege.
It is about time that the House of Commons considered transforming the letter organization of the Post Office Department into a self-sustaining, efficiently run business organization. Not for one moment do I imagine that this can be done overnight, and I do not think it should be done overnight. However, improvements should be made and thought should be directed toward establishing an efficient crown corporation that will have complete charge of all post office matters.

The Canadian post office is something more than a mere processing plant. It is not only a matter of receipts and expenditures. It also concerns the people. It is a matter of buildings and working conditions. It is also a matter of a service rendered to the entire population and to the country.
On the basis of that statement I should like to raise a question concerning the advisability of the suggestion just made by the hon. member who preceded me in this discussion. We ask whether it is absolutely necessary that a service such as this be self-sustaining in every respect. Reference has been made today to the subsidizing of other media of communication. today whether or not it is absolutely necessary to raise the rate on first class mail in order to make this phase of the operations of the Post Office Department self-sustaining. I do not believe the minister has given any proof that this operation is going to be in a deficit position. Possibly, therefore, we should have a clarification on this matter first of all.
I suggest that a further increase in postal rates will, of course, contribute once again to the increase in the cost of living. We should look at it from that point of view. speechtext:
In speaking at this time, Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to hold up the resolution or repeat anything that has already been said or the representations made to the minister. I should like to refer to one aspect of postal rates in order that the minister will be prepared to deal with the situation and provide an explanation when we consider the bill itself. I refer to the postage rates voluntary associations must bear during fund raising campaigns.
I am sure the minister has received representations from some of the voluntary fund-raising organizations in Canada, particularly those involved in health fields, regarding the increasing cost of postage. These people are contributing to the country through their services. Over the years they have been successful in their efforts to raise the funds required to provide these services at a saving to the government of both trouble and cost. As a result of the efforts of these organizations the government's contributions in many of these fields have been negative or nil.
During recent years the increase in the amount obtained through these campaigns has not kept pace with the increased cost of providing these services. The increase in cost in recent years has been substantial, particularly in respect of postage rates. Instead of letters and receipts being sent out at a two cent rate or at the bulk rate they now have to go out at the four cent rate. This has added greatly to the overhead of these organizations. One organization with which I am familiar has found that its postal costs have increased by more than 35 per cent.
It is my belief that the Post Office Department should be run efficiently but I argue with some of those who say it must be run on a business basis in order to show a profit. The hon. member for Verdun has suggested that postal services are indispensable to the unifying of this country and keeping it together. Perhaps the subsidy required today in respect of postal services is not as great
November 28, 1987

because of the improved communications available, and the use of postal services may be less in the case of some than in earlier years when it was the only means of carrying on business. In any event there are some elements of this service which must be considered seriously, particularly in respect of certain areas where rates should be maintained.
We have heard a great deal about postal rates for mail that comes in from that great country to the south. Mr. Chairman, I thought for a moment that the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard would tell the committee of the change which was made to the bill in the standing committee on transport and communications. That is why I hesitated in rising. Although it is a small change in terms of the number of words involved, it is a rather important one so far as the impact of the change upon the authority being sought by the company is concerned. In view of the fact that this change will not be considered by us until or unless we reach clause 6 of the bill, perhaps I should mention in passing that it relates to a restriction of the authority of the company with regard to the operation of aircraft, aerodromes, radios, communication systems, and the like. The company, therefore, does not seek a general licence to operate but rather authority to do so for the purpose of a particular undertaking. Thus we are not in the process of incorporating another nation-wide television or radio system by the change that has been made to the bill.
Yesterday during private members' hour the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra talked out a very reasonable resolution relating to old age pensions. In view of the fact that the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra also moved the second reading of the bill now before us and gave us an outline of it, perhaps we will fall into the habit which he established yesterday in dealing with items which come before us in private members' hour. It seems to me that if there is anything of value with which the house should concern itself it should have been the proposal relating to old age pensions moved yesterday by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
The bill before us contains two important factors. One is the authority of the company for its project and plan to establish a pipe line through which it could move solid materials, and the other is the overriding factor of Canadian ownership and involvement in this and similar companies. This subject has interested parliament for some time. To underline our interest I think it is

November 28, 1967
Private Bills
necessary to re-emphasize the declarations made by the Prime Minister regarding his desire to see a larger degree of Canadian ownership in the exploitation of our natural resources and in the industry which transforms these natural resources into usable and consumable commodities.
It is well known that the President of the Privy Council, along with many other members of the cabinet, holds this view. It is regrettable that the whole cabinet has not come to a decision on this matter because it puts us in a rather odd position in that on the one hand the first minister of the Crown has enunciated what we took to be government policy on Canadian ownership and on the other hand there is a persistent flood of bills before the house whose sponsors have ignored the declared policy of the Prime Minister, who naturally speaks for the government.
We recall the time that the Prime Minister was asked whether he spoke for the government on particular matters or whether someone else did. The Prime Minister then made it quite clear in the house that he and only he, makes announcements on behalf of the government of Caanda. As my friend the hon. member for Megantic said, these policy declarations are not always sound. I think we could spend a fair amount of time in the house speaking about the damaging features of some of the policy decisions made by the government. However, I do not wish to dwell on this matter but simply to emphasize that the Prime Minister himself declared that it is he who announces government policies and no one else.
One of the policies which he announced on a nation-wide television broadcast related to Canadian ownership. He said he was in favour of it and he hoped it would be possible to have a larger degree of Canadian ownership than exists at the present time. I do not think we can have a smaller degree of Canadian ownership in the oil industry than exists at present because I understand that the whole oil industry is foreign owned by people who have no direct political or emotional responsibility to Canada.
In the bill before us we are dealing with the oil industry, and in particular Shell Canada Limited. Some interesting aspects of the bill were placed on the record at an earlier stage of the proceedings when mention was made of the degree to which this company is the sponsor of the bill and the major shareholder in the company which the bill seeks to incorporate. The hon. member

for Vancouver Quadra in moving second reading of the bill in the early part of June this year placed this information on the record. He pointed out that Shell Canada Limited, will be the principal shareholder of Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company. The public holds 17.5 per cent of the voting power in Shell. Its shares are traded on the stock exchanges of Canada. The remaining
82.5	per cent is held by another Canadian company called Shell Investments Limited whose head office is also located in Toronto.
In looking at this situation casually we might assume that this is a Canadian owned company because it is called Shell Investments Limited, its office is located in a major Canadian city, and 17.5 per cent of its stock is traded on the market. The fact of the matter is that Shell Investments Limited is a wholly owned subsidiary of a Netherlands company located in The Hague. The ownership of the company is divided, 60 per cent in the hands of Royal Dutch Petroleum and 40 per cent in the hands of Shell Transport and Trading Company in London, England. We often find involved foreign ownership when one company is owned by another which in turn will be owned by a foreign company or a couple of other companies. The final, effective ownership of any particular company, in my opinion, must always be traced back to the company which in fact controls and operates that particular company.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
In this instance we find that Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company is in fact, in the final analysis, going to be controlled by a couple of companies, one in The Hague and the other in London, England. So far as I have been able to ascertain, there has been no indication of a desire to divest the foreign ownership structure of this enterprise.

This is quite understandable because it only became available this morning. When the bill was before that committee, it was made very clear that it was the intention of the company to make shares in the pipe line company available to other

producers in southern Alberta and to members of the public. This intention was documented before the standing committee on transport and communications.

subtopic: COMMERCIAL SOLIDS PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said, I did not have a chance to read the minutes of the proceedings before the committee. My colleagues, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and the hon. member for Timiskaming, are deeply involved in that project at the moment and undoubtedly will have an opportunity to deal with the proposition put forward in the question by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. If the hon. member is saying that this will be a Canadian owned company, then that puts an entirely different light on the situation. In that event perhaps I should curtail my remarks at this juncture. However, I rather suspect, not having heard anything to the contrary, that even though there may be an offer of shares to other producers in Alberta or to the general public, the ownership of the company will still rest in the hands of Royal Dutch and the company in England, Shell Transport and Trading Company. If I am incorrect in that assumption, perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard could, by way of another question, correct my impression. Then I could leave the matter there. Not having heard anything to the contrary I must proceed on the assumption that even though shares may be held by Canadians, effective control will still rest in the hands of someone else because, as we all know, in any corporate structure the important fact is not that you own a share or two but how many shares you hold.
I have had an opportunity of reading the first page or two of the minutes of proceedings of the committee, but I did not have an opportunity of gaining the information that was given to the committee and put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. However, some interesting information was provided by a Mr. Ritchie, who is vice president of the transport end of Shell Canada. I take it this is the same Robert Pierce Ritchie mentioned in clause 1 of the bill as one of the shareholders and promoters of this company. He pointed out that this was an important new venture in the field of transportation by pipe line. At the outset of his remarks he said, as reported on page 287 of the committee evidence:
The pipelining of solids is not a new concept. During the last 50 years short pipe lines have successfully been put into operation in England and the United States for the carriage of coal and salt.
Private Bills
More recently there have been built a 72-mile gilsonite in the United States and a 50-mile iron ore line in Tasmania. The application for the bill before you, however, represents a major advance in that the applicants contemplate construction in Canada of pipe lines many hundreds of miles in length transporting solids that have never before been moved by pipe line.
Apart from the fact that we may be embarking upon a new form of transportation which in total length surpasses what has been developed in other countries, the fact is that if the pipe line is to transport solids that have never before been moved by pipe line the assumption must be that the solids they contemplate moving have up until this time been moved by some other form of transportation. This brings us to the nub of the question of transportation policy. We know that when the massive omnibus transport bill went through parliament a while ago it was supposed to reflect a very deliberate, conscious, thought-out policy on transport following upon the heels of royal commission and interdepartmental studies of modes of transport.
I do not hold any particular brief for the maintenance of our railways but they have provided a tremendous service to some areas of the nation and have contributed tremendously to the tying together of different parts of Canada. It would seem to me that the other form of transportation which has been used to transport the solids they contemplate moving by this pipe line probably is the railways since railways can carry items in bulk quantities. It may be that truck transport or airlift from Calgary to Vancouver or some other form of transport is used. I do not believe that in this context this is really putting another form of transport into the picture in addition to those we already have. It may be that the development of the concept of moving bulk materials by pipe line which are now being moved by other forms of transport is on the increase. If so, it will undoubtedly detract from the possibility of these commodities being shipped by railway or by some other form of transport.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
My concern is about the total contribution that this may make to the well-being of the people of Canada. We all know that the Minister of Finance is supposed to have been working very hard on this during the last little while and that the greater the injection of money into certain areas of the country the greater the contribution to inflation and, if there is a duplication of services in this case,

to a potentially uneconomic situation in one or other of the forms of transport. I reiterate that I hold no particular brief for the railroads as the only means to transport commodities, but the railways may find they will have to alter their concept of transportation in order to meet this new venture which undoubtedly will confront them, whether or not this bill passes at this time.
This brings me to another extremely important aspect-

Mr. Chairman, by some coincidence, just at the point where the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard asked a question of the hon. member for Skeena-I might digress to point out that at one point in the history of our province the area which now comprises the constituency of Skeena was within the area now represented by the city of Vancouver, though that was a long time ago-I was reviewing the proceedings before the committee on transport and communications where the very point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard was dealt with.
I might say that as far as I can ascertain there is nothing in the evidence before the committee to indicate that there was anything in any way incorrect in the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena who was dealing, as I understood it, with the question of the basic ownership of the Shell oil interests in Canada and indicating that the control of those interests lies beyond the boundaries of Canada. He was not directly raising the question of the share ownership of this company except to the extent that he was indicating that this company was being sponsored by and presumably would be controlled by the Shell oil interests in this country, and therefore indirectly controlled by interests outside this country.
I have been giving serious attention to the evidence of Mr. Ritchie before the committee. He acted as their chief spokesman and is vice president, transportation, of Shell Canada Limited. As far as I am concerned the statement of Mr. Ritchie and his replies to various questions merely confirm for me the situation which someone suggested was probably the case when we dealt with the bill at the second reading stage. In the first instance, if we were to pass the bill we would be creating a company basically

foreign owned and controlled and, second, we would be perpetuating a situation which has existed in the past in the case of many oil and gas pipe line companies incorporated by acts of this parliament whereby large foreign interests maintain effective control. So far as share ownership in Canada is concerned, this would simply be a matter of throwing out a few crumbs so that a few Canadians might feel they had an interest by virtue of holding a scattered and small percentage of the share capital of these companies.
As reported on page 289 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence for Thursday, November 23 last, Mr. Ritchie said:
Prior to construction of the pipeline facilities ownership shares will be offered to other sulphur producers in Alberta as well as the public. Following start-up and proven success, a further public offering of shares to Canadians will be made by the owner-producers.
Prior to making those remarks Mr. Ritchie had pointed out that the estimated cost of the line is $60 million. He stated that while research is under way the Shell oil company is bearing the full financial burden of this phase. So I think it is very evident that the situation as outlined by the hon. member for Skeena is a correct analysis.
As reported on page 292 of the evidence, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace Mr. Ritchie said:
As we envisage Commercial Solids Pipe Line Company, it would be owned by a number of shareholders, including the public. However the producers would all want a share interest in it, and once they had that, I would think they would continue to support it.
This question relates generally to a pipe line operating as a transport concern which is affected by potential competition by the railways.
As reported on page 295 of the committee's proceedings, the hon. member for Kindersley asked this question:
I am interested too in what you said about the shares being offered to the public. Would you care to give us an opinion as to how soon, if you get the pipe line into operation, these shares would be offered, and perhaps what percentage of capitalization might then be offered to the public?
Mr. Ritchie replied:
You are asking two questions. Relating to the first one, we would envisage that there would be some shares offered to the public at the inception. We try to spell this out in that very short statement. This is a new project. We feel that it would not necessarily be in the public interest to have a large share in the hands of the public at the inception. As soon as the project is operating and
November 28, 1967

there is no question as to its success and the statement is made, we would have an offering and expect that there would be additional shares offered to the public.
Once you have the public in a facility, even though it is a very small percentage of the public, you have to operate the facility in the public interest and not in the interest of the producers. So really the total number of shareholders I do not think really makes that much difference in the way the facility would be operated.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
That leads us back to a point which was raised previously in this house on a number of occasions with respect to the operation of pipe line companies. In sponsoring this pipe line company, Shell wishes to perpetuate a situation that has existed in Canada with respect to the transmission by pipe line of gas and oil. It boils down to this: The major producers such as Shell, Imperial or B.A. maintain effective control and management of pipe line companies and retain the bulk of the shares. While a small percentage of shares is made available to the Canadian public, allegations that pipe lines, such as the one proposed in this bill, operate in the public interest are highly debatable, to say the least.
Mr. Ritchie's statement did nothing to allay my fears. Rather, it confirmed my suspicion that the proposition which was being put before us would perpetuate the intolerable situation in the pipe line transportation field. Some may argue that we have gone too far with respect to transmission by pipe line to turn back now, but I am not prepared to admit that that is so. In other words, I think we are now entering a new phase of transportation by pipe line. This is an opportune time for parliament to examine again the entire question of pipe line transportation. In this field we need not perpetuate the mistakes we have made in the past. I refer particularly to those mistakes we have made since the end of world war II and to the manner in which we allowed pipe line transmission systems for gas and oil to develop.
The hon. member for Jacques-Cartier-Lasalle, who was one of the committee members, asked Mr. Ritchie about Shell's interest, generally, in pipe lines. The answer confirms what I have said. Shell seeks to perpetuate a situation that exists with respect to the transmission of oil and gas by pipe line.

Indeed, I was surprised to learn, when I received the report, that none of the government departments which would normally be concerned with the subject of this measure was represented before the committee. I was surprised that the Department of Transport did not suggest that the Canadian National Railways should intervene in this application. I would have thought that several other government agencies would have been interested in attending, not necessarily to oppose the bill but to bring out the relationship which this company could have with other agencies in the transportation field.
I was interested in the way in which the chairman introduced the statement of the Minister of Transport. Rather than ask that the minister be present, he read a letter from the minister. I was surprised at the statement made by the minister to the effect that while

this proposed pipe line would come under the new transportation legislation, part II of that legislation had not yet been proclaimed. And he gave no indication of when part II relating to pipe lines would be put into effect.
I had been of the opinion that the whole of the legislation would have been proclaimed by the governor in council at the same time. I understand now that it is likely that this matter will be dealt with within a few months. In the meantime I presume the present application is having some effect on the date of proclamation. The operation referred to in the bill before us should, I believe, be classed as a commodity pipe line, thereby bringing it into the transportation field.
I noticed on reading the annual report of the National Energy Board that it is very pleased with the growth of Canadian oil production. Since the late 'fifties the production level has about doubled. The statement goes on to say that Canada's petroleum resources have been extended even more rapidly, a development which poses an urgent need for further expansion of markets for Canadian oil. As we are well aware, Shell Oil is interested in this type of pipe line operation because of the problem created by the large residue of sulphur left after oil refining. Sulphur is a commodity which is rather difficult to transport. As the committee report indicates, the transportation cost to the railway is $10 plus an additional $2 in handling charges. The company is of the opinion that transporting the sulphur by means of a slurry operation in an oil carrier would reduce the cost of transportation considerably below that level.
There is an indication that 5,000 cars of sulphur need to be transported. Since I am not in a position to know the total transportation costs involved, I am not able to determine whether or not they constitute an important factor in the operation of the railway as far as revenue is concerned. But in establishing the transportation commission the government obviously took the view that all the transportation facilities in Canada should be united under the control of one commissioner, so as to improve transportation for the Canadian people and reduce costs to producers and consumers.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think most hon. members know the purpose of this measure. Its purpose is to make sure that federal government employees in all parts of Canada and elsewhere are covered by this legislation, the Government Employees Compensation Act.
This act really is the counterpart of the workmen's compensation acts of the different provinces. In the Northwest Territories and the Yukon government employees are covered by arrangements with the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia under their workmen's compensation acts. Certain situations have arisen as a result of comprehensive new programs introduced by the present government. Among others I might mention retraining programs under way in technical schools.
The purpose of this bill is to extend coverage so as to cover not only federal employees, but federal employees who cease work to take training or retraining courses. The second part of the bill relates to employees in our foreign services, employees of the Department of External Affairs, of the Department of Trade and Commerce and latterly the Department of Labour. The Department of Labour now has a number of employees posted to several key places outside Canada.

It should be pointed out that when these federal government employees go to countries in Asia and Africa they are subject to certain tropical diseases, unless they have built up an immunity. Mr. Chairman, I would have liked to make some remarks and put a few questions to the minister about clause 3 of Bill No. C-151.
In the absence of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer)-I do not see him in his seat at present-I think it would be appropriate, especially after what happened in early November, to ask ourselves a few questions about the future of the C.N.R. It will be recalled that on November 1, practically without warning, the C.N.R. decided to lay off a great number of employees, most of whom were taken completely unawares. The reason given then was that those lay-ofls were mainly due to a decrease in railway traffic.
Mr. Chairman, I do not know exactly what the situation is in other areas of the country, but so far as northwestern Quebec is concerned, when 127 section-men are laid off in a rather small area compared to the full railway network we tend to wonder what the C.N.R. is up to; we also wonder if this crown corporation did not give this reason to lay off its employees simply to get around a clause in the contract negotiated with the union representing the section-men.
So, Mr. Chairman, when we realize what is happening-and I am speaking mostly of northwestern Quebec-it does not seem that railroad traffic is falling off when new industries are being set up.
Recently, a paper and pulp mill started operations. I am sure that when a mill such

DEBATES	November 28, 1967
as this one, which represents outlays of over $75 million, starts producing and shipping products there is an increase in shipments by rail, and not a decrease. In the mining industry for instance, shipments between various points are as high now as they were last summer or last year.
Consequently, Mr. Chairman, people wonder. I have here letters from presidents of railroad unions, from railroaders, who are alarmed, and rightly so, at this massive layoff which has spread confusion and chaos amongst the employees. I feel that the Canadian National should at least have notified its employees a few weeks ahead of time; it might have spared them considerable losses in time and money, e (8:40 p.m.)
I should like at this stage to put on the official record the following letter, which I received from president of local 399 of the Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen, Mr. Leonard Gilbert; I quote:
Dear sir:
Following our interview in your La Sarre office, I would ask you to find out whether the C.N.R. lay-offs which took place on November 1, on only 3 or 4 days' notice, were intended to annoy the employees, or whether, after calculating approximately the loss in time involved, the C.N.R. decided that it would save the same amount of money by not paying the salaries of the workers.
If we had only had 2 weeks' notice, the loss in time could have been reduced to a maximum of 1 or 2 days. Had Quebec been chosen as the centre for these operations, everyone would have known where to go according to seniority, before the date scheduled for these lay-offs, whereas, since no notice was given, some workers were moved two or three times, and time was lost between each move.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the problem raised by such a lay-off without notice. As these employees are entitled to seniority, vacancies in the maintenance sections of the track were filled by other employees, while the employees laid off, not knowing exactly where to go, had to move two or three times, and had to suffer loss of time and money each time. However the Canadian National may have succeeded in saving a few dollars.
Because of that situation, I think that the president of local 399 is justified in complaining and in insisting that, in the future, if a lay-off is necessary, notice should be given long enough in advance so that the employees transfer centre has enough time to inform those who have to change job, so that they can do so without losing too much time.
I also have a letter from Mr. Louis Boudreau, president of local 328 in Senneterre, which is just as hard on the C.N.R. I will
